shortlist.raw_text: With the rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), evaluating their video understanding capabilities has become increasingly important. Existing video understanding benchmarks cover only part of the evaluation dimensions, limiting systematic diagnosis of omni-modal video understanding. We introduce OmniCompass, a holistic benchmark for omni-modal video grounding and understanding. OmniCompass defines two evaluation tracks: OmniCompass-VL assesses vision-language models on tasks requiring visual evidence, while OmniCompass-AV assesses omni-modal models on tasks requiring joint audio-visual evidence. Each track includes three complementary tasks: temporal grounding (TG), spatial grounding (SG), and question answering (QA), assessing when a referenced target appears, where it is, and what happens. QA covers five perception and three reasoning categories in OmniCompass-VL, and three perception and two reasoning categories in OmniCompass-AV. OmniCompass-VL contains 820 videos and 2,460 instances across domains and three duration types: short, medium, and long. A narrative- and audio-rich subset forms OmniCompass-AV with 240 videos and 720 instances. Each instance is evaluated under two paired settings: text-only and text+image, specifying the same target through text and visual-language guidance. All instances are manually annotated with multi-round quality verification. Evaluations of 50 MLLMs show that open-source models still lag behind proprietary counterparts, particularly in audio-visual understanding. Precise temporal and spatial grounding remains challenging even for leading models, and their predictions still exhibit inconsistencies across the paired target specifications.

shortlist.raw_text: Policy-shift distillation reuses the difference between a teacher's log probabilities before and after reinforcement learning (RL) as supervision on student-generated trajectories. However, this endpoint policy shift cannot reveal whether local action preferences evolved consistently during teacher training. The same endpoint shift can result from early and late shifts that reinforce or partially cancel each other. We investigate whether agreement between early and late teacher policy shifts can guide selective transfer. We introduce Waypoint-guided On-Policy Distillation (Waypoint-OPD), which uses an intermediate teacher checkpoint from the same RL run to compare early and late shifts in relative action preferences at student-visited prefixes. We gate the endpoint shift according to the directional agreement between the early and late shifts, suppressing it when they point in opposing directions. Compared with endpoint-only transfer, our method requires only one additional frozen-teacher scoring pass. Using RL-trained Qwen3-4B teachers, we evaluate our method with Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Qwen3-30B-A3B as student models in mathematical and code reasoning. In all six domain--student settings, Waypoint-OPD achieves the highest domain-average score among the compared distillation methods. Ablations with the Qwen3-8B student show that removing or shuffling gates reduces mathematical reasoning performance. These results support the use of directional agreement between early and late teacher policy shifts to weight the endpoint shift during student training.

shortlist.raw_text: Harness self-evolution revises an agent's software scaffolding, including prompts, memory, workflows, and executable components, while keeping model weights fixed. We formalize a feedback-driven process in which accepted revisions persist across runs. The framework separates update targets from proposal and admission mechanisms. It distinguishes changes to interpreted state from revisions to tools and code, repository-level control logic, and plugin composition. We characterize search through evolutionary optimization and examine its reliability through continual PAC-learning. Under explicit assumptions, the analysis yields an expected generalization bound, a retention bound conditional on historical regression budgets, and a high-probability admission rule using fresh, independent validation data. We examine how persistent harness revisions affect knowledge sharing and organizational workflows, with implications for scientific reliability, physical safety, and institutional accountability. Cases from prior work illustrate model--harness co-design, distributed execution, and plugin reuse. Reliable deployment requires continual validation as task distributions and evaluators change, with independent safeguards for learning, runtime privileges, and consequential actions. We provide a comprehensive 66-page discussion of related work, theory, algorithms, evaluation, applications, and the broader impact of Harness RSI, together with continuously updated code and supplementary materials, at https://github.com/zgcagi/Harness-RSI.

OpenAI’s ChatGPT Atlas browser is gone , but now ChatGPT’s Google Chrome extension is getting some upgrades that allow it to use the browser tabs you already have open. With the extension installed, OpenAI says ChatGPT can now view your browser tabs when you tag Chrome in ChatGPT’s web or desktop app, posting a demo video showing someone asking ChatGPT to compare the three tabs they have open with sofas they’re considering.

It’s also updated ChatGPT in the sidebar , with “the full power of ChatGPT” and your entire conversation history in Chat or Work to use without leaving the page you’re viewing. It also enables ChatGPT Work to “control” your Chrome tabs for tasks like “sending messages, filling out forms, or downloading files,” similar to Google’s Gemini-powered “auto browse” feature , as well as organize or group open tabs.

Research notes on: OpenAI updated its ChatGPT Google Chrome extension to allow the AI to view, analyze, and control open browser tabs.
(Found by web search. Some coverage may be older background. Use it for context and explanation, but don't present older events as new, and keep the main story's facts primary.)

Coverage from NewsBytes: "ChatGPT can now work across your open Chrome tabs"
OpenAI's ChatGPT extension for Google Chrome now allows the AI to access and utilize information from your open browser tabs, enhancing its functionality and user experience.

Coverage from Windows Report on MSN: "ChatGPT can now access Chrome tabs and automate browser tasks"
OpenAI upgrades its ChatGPT Chrome extension with tab access, browser automation, and ChatGPT Work integration.

Coverage from UA.NEWS: "OpenAI updates ChatGPT extension for Chrome with access to open tabs — The Verge"
OpenAI has updated the ChatGPT extension for Google Chrome: it can use information from open browser tabs and also work in the sidebar. This was reported by The Verge .
According to OpenAI, after installing the extension, a user can select Chrome in the web version or desktop app of ChatGPT so that the chatbot can view open tabs. In a demonstration, a user asks the AI to compare three pages featuring sofas they are considering buying.
The company also provided examples of prompts for the updated extension. In particular, ChatGPT can use information from an event description to fill out a registration form and stop before submitting it. Another example involves comparing contractors' services in open tabs and drafting an email to the company that best meets home renovation needs.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram .
The proposed scenarios also include filling out a form before a dentist visit while simultaneously adding the appointment to work and personal calendars.
OpenAI has also updated ChatGPT in Chrome's sidebar. It offers a full history of conversations with the chatbot and Chat and Work interfaces that can be used without leaving the open page.
In ChatGPT Work, the tool can manage Chrome tabs for tasks such as sending messages, filling out forms, or uploading files. In addition, it can organize and group open tabs. The Verge compares these capabilities to the auto browse feature in Google's Gemini-powered browser.

Background (Browser extension, Wikipedia):
A browser extension is a software module for customizing a web browser. Browsers typically allow users to install a variety of extensions, including user interface modifications, cookie management, ad blocking, and custom scripting and styling of web pages.

Background (Headless browser, Wikipedia):
A headless browser is a web browser without a graphical user interface.

text:
ChatGPT can now read every tab you have open in Chrome.

You just tag Chrome in the app, and the model pulls the data straight from your browser.

Here is what the update actually changes.

OpenAI just rolled out a new Chrome extension.

It gives the chatbot direct access to your open browser tabs.

In their demo, a user asks the AI to compare three separate tabs of sofas they are considering.

The features go past simple reading.
• Pulling info from an event description to fill out a registration form
• Comparing contractor services in open tabs to draft an email
• Managing tabs by grouping and organizing them directly
• Controlling browser actions like sending messages or uploading files

Google already has a similar auto browse feature in Gemini.

My read: browser extensions are becoming the real operating system.

The catch is obvious. The feature relies entirely on OpenAI's own claims and demo videos.

How many open tabs are you willing to hand over to a chatbot?

Source: The Verge, with reporting from NewsBytes and Windows Report on MSN
